sections.title: How to work through the projects

blocks.text:
Reading about Java is not the same as building with it. Interviewers and teammates trust people who have finished programs, not people who know the vocabulary. This Part gives you four projects, each small enough to finish in an evening or two and each chosen to exercise a different slice of the book: object-oriented design and file persistence, streams and java.time, concurrency, and data structures with locking. Every listing was compiled and run on a JDK 21 build machine and the output shown is the real output.

### Ground rules shared by all four projects

Each project uses the same conventions, so you only learn them once.

- **Plain tools only.** You need `javac` and `java`, nothing else. Maven, Gradle and JUnit are what you would use at work (see the chapters on testing and packaging in Part 11), but a project you cannot build without downloading half the internet is hard to study.
- **Package per project.** Code lives under `com.example.<project>`, split into sub-packages by role (`model`, `repo`, `service`, `app`). The directory structure must mirror the package names.
- **Sources and tests are separate trees.** `src/` holds production code, `test/` holds tests. Compiled classes go to `out/` and `testout/`, which you can delete at any time.
- **Time and randomness are injected.** Code that calls `LocalDate.now()` or `new Random()` directly cannot be tested. Our classes take a `Clock` (see the java.time chapter) or a seed, so the output in this book is repeatable.
- **A hand-rolled test runner.** JUnit is not assumed to be installed, so every project ships a tiny runner (about 40 lines) that registers named checks, runs them, prints PASS/FAIL and sets the process exit code. You will read it once in the first project and reuse the idea afterwards.
- **Scripted input.** Interactive programs read from `System.in`. We feed them a text file with shell redirection (`<` `script.txt`), which makes demos reproducible and also makes the program testable.

### The standard workflow

For each project, work in this order. It mirrors how professional work goes, just faster.

1. Read the goal and the design section. Draw the classes on paper before reading code.
2. Create the directory tree, then type the files in. Typing, not pasting, is what makes you notice details.
3. Compile. Fix errors one at a time, reading the first error message only; later ones are often consequences.
4. Run the program with the scripted input and compare with the output in the book.
5. Run the tests. Then break something on purpose (change a `>` to `>=`) and watch a test fail. A test you have never seen fail proves little.
6. Do at least one extension idea from the end of the chapter without looking for a solution.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: The compile command used throughout is `javac -d out $(find src -name '*.java')`. The `-d out` flag tells javac where to put `.class` files and it creates the package directories for you. On Windows PowerShell use `javac -d out` `(Get-ChildItem -Recurse src -Filter *.java).FullName`.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The projects deliberately avoid frameworks, but they follow the layering you will meet in Spring Boot: a controller-like entry point (`app`), a service layer with the business rules, a repository interface hiding storage, and plain model classes. When you reach Spring later, you will recognise every box.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Every project: plain javac, `src` and `test` trees, package per project with role sub-packages.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Inject `Clock` and seeds so behaviour is repeatable and testable.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Scripted input plus a tiny test runner make console programs verifiable without any framework.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Break something on purpose to prove your tests can fail.

sections.title: Project A: A bank account manager

blocks.text:
### Goal

Build a console program that opens accounts, deposits, withdraws, transfers between accounts, prints statements and remembers everything between runs. It looks like a toy, but it exercises most of Part 3 (classes, interfaces, enums, records, immutability, exceptions) plus collections and NIO file handling. The same design works for an inventory app (items instead of accounts, stock instead of balance); see the extension ideas.

Requirements:

- Accounts have an id, an owner and a type. A savings account may overdraw by up to 5.00; a checking account may not.
- Money is stored as whole cents in a `long`. Never use `double` for money (see the numbers chapter in Part 4).
- Business failures (not enough money) and input mistakes (negative amount, unknown account) are reported differently.
- Data is stored in a CSV file and survives restarts. A crash during saving must not corrupt the file.
- A text menu reads commands such as `deposit AC001 25.25`.

### Design

blocks.caption: The layers used in every project: the entry point talks to services, services talk to a storage interface, and model classes are shared by all layers. Dependencies point downward only.
blocks.alt: Main / CLI (entry point) | Model classes | records, enums, | Services (business rules) exceptions | (shared by all) | Storage interface -> file / in-memory | dependencies point downward only

blocks.text:
Responsibilities, from bottom to top:

- **model**: `Account` (mutable state with rules), `AccountType` (enum carrying the overdraft limit), `Transaction` (immutable record), `Money` (parse and format cents), and two exceptions.
- **repo**: the `Repository<T, ID>` interface and two implementations. `InMemoryAccountRepository` keeps a `TreeMap` so listings are sorted by id. `FileAccountRepository` loads a CSV at start and rewrites it after every save.
- **service**: `BankService` holds the use cases (open, deposit, withdraw, transfer). It depends on the `Repository` interface, not on a concrete class, so tests can use the in-memory version.
- **app**: `Main` parses command lines and prints results. No business rule lives here.

Two design decisions deserve a sentence each. First, `InsufficientFundsException` is **checked** because running out of money is a normal outcome that every caller must handle; `InvalidAmountException` extends `IllegalArgumentException` (unchecked) because a negative amount is a bug or bad input, not an outcome to plan for (see the exceptions chapter in Part 5). Second, `Transaction` is a **record** because it is pure immutable data.

### The code

Create the tree below. All paths are relative to the project directory.

src/com/example/bank/model/Transaction.java

blocks.title: Project layout

blocks.text: We start with the small model types.

blocks.title: AccountType.java
Transaction.java
Money.java
Gotcha
blocks.text: `Money.parse("1.5")` is rejected on purpose. Accepting one decimal digit invites the bug where "1.5" becomes 105 cents. Being strict at the boundary is cheaper than debugging wrong balances later. Note also `Math.multiplyExact` and `Math.addExact`: they throw `ArithmeticException` on overflow instead of silently wrapping around (see the numbers chapters), and we translate that into our own exception.
The two exceptions show the checked versus unchecked choice in code.

blocks.title: InsufficientFundsException.java
InvalidAmountException.java

blocks.text: Now the central class, `Account`.

blocks.title: Account.java

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- Fields are `private`; the only way to change the balance is `deposit` or `withdraw`, so the rules cannot be bypassed (encapsulation).
- `history()` returns `Collections.unmodifiableList(history)`, a read-only view. Without it a caller could call `account.history().clear()` and erase the audit trail. A test checks this.
- `withdraw` checks the rule before changing any state, then updates balance and history together. The order matters: if validation threw after the balance changed, the object would be left inconsistent.
- `restore` is a named factory used only when loading from disk. A comment says history is not persisted; that is a known limitation we list under extensions.

Next the storage layer: one interface, two implementations.

blocks.title: Repository.java
InMemoryAccountRepository.java
FileAccountRepository.java

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `findById` returns `Optional`, so "not found" cannot be confused with a `null` bug.
- `FileAccountRepository` reuses the in-memory version as a cache (composition over inheritance). Only `save` touches the disk.
- `flush` writes `accounts.csv.tmp` and then moves it over the real file with `ATOMIC_MOVE`. If the program dies mid-write, the old file is still intact. This is the standard "write temp, then rename" pattern (see the NIO.2 chapter in Part 5).
- Both IO methods convert `IOException` into `UncheckedIOException` with a clear message and the original cause. The repository interface stays free of checked IO exceptions, so services need not know the storage is a file.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: `ATOMIC_MOVE` is not supported on every file system and combining it with `REPLACE_EXISTING` may be ignored on some platforms. It works on normal local disks on Linux, macOS and Windows. If you target network drives, catch `AtomicMoveNotSupportedException` and fall back to a plain replace.
The service holds the use cases.

blocks.title: BankService.java

blocks.text:
The important method is `transfer`. It looks up **both** accounts before changing either, so an unknown destination cannot leave money withdrawn. It withdraws first because that is the step that can fail with the checked exception; the deposit cannot fail after that. In a real database you would use a transaction instead of relying on step order (see the extension ideas for a rollback exercise).

Finally the text menu.

blocks.title: Main.java

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- The `switch` is the arrow form with no fall-through. The method returns `false` for `quit`, which ends the loop.
- Two catch blocks give two behaviours: a checked business failure prints `DECLINED`, input and lookup mistakes print `ERROR`. One bad command never kills the program.
- The constructor takes an `InputStream`, so a test could pass a `ByteArrayInputStream`.

### Running it

Save the commands below as `script1.txt`. Each line is typed into the menu; some are deliberately wrong.

**script1.txt**

open Ravi savings 20.50
deposit AC001 25.25
withdraw AC001 500
transfer AC001 AC002 50
withdraw AC002 99.99
deposit AC002 -5
deposit AC009 5
deposit AC001 abc
list
history AC001
quit

$ rm -rf out accounts.csv
$ javac -d out $(find src -name '*.java')
$ java -cp out com.example.bank.app.Main accounts.csv < script1.txt

opened AC001 [CHECKING] Asha 100.00
> open Ravi savings 20.50
opened AC002 [SAVINGS] Ravi 20.50
> deposit AC001 25.25
> withdraw AC001 500
DECLINED: account AC001 is short by 374.75
> transfer AC001 AC002 50
> withdraw AC002 99.99
DECLINED: account AC002 is short by 24.49

ERROR: amount must be positive, got -5.00
> deposit AC009 5
ERROR: no account AC009
> deposit AC001 abc
ERROR: bad amount: 'abc'
> list
  AC001 [CHECKING] Asha 75.25
  AC002 [SAVINGS] Ravi 70.50
> history AC001
  2026-03-01 DEPOSIT           25.25  balance     125.25
  2026-03-01 WITHDRAW          50.00  balance      75.25

blocks.title: Compile and run the scripted session

blocks.text:
Look at each declined or failed line. The 500.00 withdrawal is declined with the exact shortfall (checking accounts have no overdraft). The savings account may dip 5.00 below zero, so withdrawing 99.99 from 70.50 is short by 24.49, not 29.49. Negative amounts, unknown accounts and the text "abc" are all reported without crashing.

The data file is plain text and the second run proves persistence.

AC002,Ravi,SAVINGS,7050
$ printf 'list\nwithdraw AC001 1000\nquit\n' | java -cp out com.example.bank.app.Main accounts.csv

  AC002 [SAVINGS] Ravi 70.50

DECLINED: account AC001 is short by 924.75

blocks.text:
### Tests with a hand-rolled runner

Here is the whole test framework. It is intentionally tiny: tests are named lambdas; `assertThrows` takes the expected exception type.

blocks.title: MiniTest.java

blocks.text: Tests use it like JUnit, except they are registered in `main`.

blocks.title: BankTests.java

blocks.code:
$ javac -d testout -cp out $(find test -name '*.java')
$ java -cp out:testout com.example.bank.BankTests
PASS Money.parse handles whole and fractional amounts
PASS Money.parse rejects one-decimal input
PASS Money.format round-trips negatives
PASS deposit increases balance and records history
PASS withdraw beyond balance throws checked exception
PASS savings may overdraw up to the limit
PASS failed transfer changes neither account
PASS history view cannot be modified
PASS file repository survives a restart
9 tests, 0 failed
$ echo "exit code: $?"
exit code: 0
blocks.title: Compile and run the tests
Note
blocks.text: On Windows the classpath separator is `;` instead of `:`.

#### What the tests cover

Pure helpers (parsing and formatting), the happy path, the checked exception, the overdraft rule, the all-or-nothing property of `transfer`, the read-only history and persistence across a "restart" (a second repository reading the same file). Each test builds its own fresh bank so tests cannot affect each other; that independence is the single most important property of a test suite.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why is money stored as a `long` of cents rather than `double` or `BigDecimal`? `double` cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly (0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3), so sums drift. `BigDecimal` is exact and is the right tool when you need arbitrary scale or rounding rules. Whole minor units in a `long` are exact, fast and simple when the currency has a fixed number of decimals, and `Math.addExact` guards overflow. Many payment systems store minor units for exactly this reason.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In a Spring Boot version, `BankService` becomes a `@Service`, `Repository` becomes a Spring Data repository backed by a database table, and `transfer` gets `@Transactional` so that both legs commit or roll back together. The shape of the code stays the same.

### Extension ideas

1. **Inventory variant.** Replace `Account` with `Item` (sku, name, quantity) and `withdraw` with `remove`; throwing a checked `OutOfStockException`. Add a `low` command that lists items under a threshold using a stream.
2. Persist the transaction history too (one line per transaction in a second file) and load it in `restore`.
3. Make `transfer` genuinely atomic: if `repo.save(dst)` fails after `repo.save(src)`, undo the first save.
4. Add a monthly interest method on savings accounts using `BigDecimal` with `RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN`, and test the rounding.
5. Add a `Statement` formatter that prints a table using a text block template and `String.formatted`.
6. Replace the CSV with a JSON-lines file written by hand, then think about what a library such as Jackson would save you.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Layers (app, service, repo, model) keep rules in one place and storage replaceable behind an interface.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Store money in minor units; use `Math.*Exact`; validate at the boundary.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Checked exceptions for expected business outcomes, unchecked for bad input and bugs.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Write-then-rename makes file persistence crash-safe; read-only views protect internal state.

sections.title: Project B: A log file analyzer

blocks.text:
### Goal

Operations people read logs for a living, and "count the errors per hour and show me the slow endpoints" is a question you will answer with code many times. This project builds a command-line analyzer that reads a web-server style log, tolerates bad lines, and prints a report. It exercises regular expressions, `java.time`, the Stream API with collectors, `Optional`, records, text blocks and `Files.lines`.

Because we have no real log, the project also contains a **generator** that writes a reproducible fake one. Seeding `java.util.Random` makes the same seed produce the same file on every machine, which is what makes the report below repeatable.

The log format, one entry per line:

**Log line format**

blocks.code:
2026-03-01T08:00:01.131Z INFO  [billing] PUT /orders 200 17ms user=u13
timestamp(UTC)           level service   method path   status latency user

blocks.text:
### Design

- **model**: `Level` enum (ordered DEBUG to ERROR) and `LogEntry` record. The record has a derived `endpoint()` that turns `GET /orders/42` and `GET /orders/77` into the same key `GET /orders/{id}`. Without this grouping, every id would be its own "endpoint".
- **io**: `LogGenerator` writes the file; `LogParser` turns one line into an `Optional<LogEntry>`.
- **analysis**: `Analyzer` runs all the statistics and returns an immutable `Report` record.
- **app**: `Main` formats the report with a text block.

Two design choices to notice. The parser returns `Optional` instead of throwing, because malformed lines are expected in real logs and should be counted, not fatal. And the report is **data** (a record), not printed text; formatting lives only in `Main`. That separation is what lets the tests assert on numbers rather than on strings.

### The code

#### Model

blocks.title: Level.java
LogEntry.java

blocks.text: #### The generator

blocks.title: LogGenerator.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: `new Random(seed)` gives a fixed sequence; every 97th line is replaced with garbage so we can test error handling; latencies follow an exponential distribution (`-Math.log(1 - u)` times a mean), which resembles real latency data with a long tail; 5xx responses get an extra 300 ms. The format string uses `%-5s` to pad the level and `Instant.toString()` for the timestamp, which is always ISO-8601 in UTC.

#### The parser

blocks.title: LogParser.java

blocks.text: The regular expression uses **named groups** (`(?<status>\d{3})`) read with `m.group("status")`. Named groups survive edits to the pattern; numbered groups break silently when you add one. The pattern is a `static final Pattern`, compiled once: compiling inside the per-line method would repeat the work two thousand times. `matches()` requires the whole line to fit the pattern, and `^...$` makes the intent explicit.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: The `catch` covers `IllegalArgumentException` because `Level.valueOf("LOUD")` throws it, and `NumberFormatException` (a subclass) from a number that does not fit an `int`. `DateTimeParseException` is not a subclass of it, so both appear in the multi-catch (which forbids listing a class and its own subclass together).
#### The analyzer

blocks.title: Report.java
Analyzer.java

blocks.text:
Walk through the collectors, because they are the point of this project (see the collectors chapter in Part 7).

- `groupingBy(LogEntry::level, () -> new TreeMap<>(), counting())` counts entries per level. The map factory argument picks a `TreeMap`, so keys come out in enum declaration order instead of hash order.
- Top endpoints: group by endpoint, then stream the map's `entrySet()`, sort by count descending with ties broken by key (so output is deterministic), and `limit(5)`. `comparingByValue().reversed()` needs the explicit type witness `Map.Entry.<String, Long>` because Java cannot infer the type through the chained call.
- `averagingInt` computes the mean per service in one pass.
- p95 sorts latencies into a `long[]` and picks the element at rank `ceil(0.95 * n)`. This "nearest rank" definition is simple and common; other definitions interpolate and give slightly different numbers.
- `truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.HOURS)` rounds an `Instant` down to the hour, which makes a natural grouping key for errors per hour.
- `partitioningBy` always produces both keys (`true` and `false`), even if one group is empty, so `get(true)` never returns `null`.
- `.flatMap(Optional::stream)` is the idiom for "keep the present values, drop the empties" (Java 9+).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: `Files.lines` holds an open file handle until the stream is closed. Always wrap it in try-with-resources as shown. Forgetting it leaks file descriptors, and on Windows it can stop you deleting the file.
#### The report printer

blocks.title: Main.java

blocks.text:
The text block uses `%s` and `%d` placeholders and `.formatted(...)` (see the strings chapter). The closing `"""` sits at the left margin of the content, which defines how much indentation is stripped. Each section is first built into a string with `Collectors.joining("\n")`, a common way to turn a collection into multi-line text.

blocks.text:
Since the generator is seeded, you should see the same numbers. If you change the seed, every figure changes but the invariants hold: the level counts sum to the number of entries, and the successes plus failures equal the same total.

### Tests

The tests reuse the `MiniTest` runner from the previous project (copy it into the `com.example.logs` test package). Two things are worth studying: the first test builds data by hand so every expected value can be computed on paper (100 latencies of 1 to 100 ms, so the 95th-percentile by nearest rank is exactly 95), and the generator test proves determinism by writing the same seed twice and comparing the files.

blocks.title: LogTests.java

blocks.code:
$ javac -d testout -cp out $(find test -name '*.java')
$ java -cp out:testout com.example.logs.LogTests

PASS parse rejects garbage and bad timestamps
PASS p95 and failure partition on a hand-made list
PASS errors are grouped by hour
PASS generator is deterministic and analyzer counts bad lines
PASS Level.atLeast follows declaration order
6 tests, 0 failed
blocks.title: Run the tests
Interview angle
blocks.text: How would you compute a top-N of a very large log file that does not fit in memory? Stream the file line by line (`Files.lines`), never collect all lines, and keep only counters. If the number of distinct keys also does not fit, use an approximate structure (count-min sketch) or process in partitions: hash each key to one of K temporary files, count each partition separately, then merge the top-N. For the in-memory case, a size-N min-heap (`PriorityQueue`) beats sorting everything.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Real systems rarely analyze log files with hand-written code; they ship structured JSON logs to Elasticsearch, Loki or similar. But the same operations (parse, group by a time bucket, percentile) are exactly what dashboards perform, and log parsing code still appears in migration scripts and incident investigations.

### Extension ideas

1. Add command-line options: `--min-level WARN` using `Level.atLeast`, and `--service billing`, applied as stream filters before the statistics.
2. Parse the file in parallel with `lines.parallel()` and compare timings with the sequential version. Is it faster for 2000 lines? For 5 million? Explain why (see the parallel streams discussion in Part 7).
3. Add a "busiest minute" statistic (group by `truncatedTo(MINUTES)`, take the `max` by value).
4. Support a second log format by introducing a `LineFormat` interface with two implementations and choosing by a command-line flag.
5. Print an ASCII bar chart of errors per hour using `"#".repeat(n)`.
6. Detect bursts: report any 5-minute window containing more than 10 errors (sliding window over sorted timestamps).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Return `Optional` from parsers of untrusted input and count the empties instead of crashing.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Collectors (`groupingBy`, `counting`, `averagingInt`, `partitioningBy`) express reports declaratively; pass a map factory when key order matters.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Keep results as data (records) and formatting separate so tests check numbers.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Always close `Files.lines` streams, and compile regex `Pattern` objects once.

sections.title: Project C: A concurrent order processor

blocks.text:
### Goal

A shop receives orders and must validate and charge each one. Each charge involves a slow call to a payment service, so one order takes about 10 ms of waiting, not computing. Processing 200 orders one by one takes over two seconds; processing them concurrently should take a fraction of that. This project implements the same job **five ways** and checks that all five agree:

1. sequentially (the baseline),
2. with a hand-built producer-consumer pipeline on a `BlockingQueue`,
3. with an `ExecutorService` thread pool and `Future`s,
4. with `CompletableFuture` stages,
5. with Java 21 virtual threads.

It also shows a graceful shutdown, a deliberate data race, and a test strategy for concurrent code. Read the concurrency Part first (threads, the memory model, executors, CompletableFuture, virtual threads); this chapter applies it.

### Design

The work itself is separated from the way it is scheduled. That is the main design idea: `OrderProcessor.process(Order)` knows nothing about threads, and each `Runner` implementation decides how to call it for many orders.

- **model**: `Order` and `Result` records, and `Summary`, an order-independent digest (counts plus a checksum of ids). Concurrent runs finish in unpredictable order, so we cannot compare result lists directly. A summary that ignores order lets us ask "did every runner produce the same outcome?".
- **work**: `OrderGenerator` (seeded) and `OrderProcessor`, which sleeps for the simulated latency and then applies two business rules: reject amounts over 900.00, reject customers whose name ends in 13.
- **run**: the `Runner` interface and five implementations.
- **app**: `Main` times all runners; `ShutdownDemo` and `RaceDemo` illustrate two ideas separately.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Using `Thread.sleep` to imitate I/O is a deliberate simplification. A sleeping thread, like a thread blocked on a socket, uses no CPU. That is the situation where more threads than cores help. For CPU-bound work (hashing, image resizing) a pool larger than the core count gains nothing.

### The code

#### Model and work

blocks.code:
package com.example.orders.model;
public record Order(int id, String customer, long amountCents) { }
blocks.title: Order.java
Result.java
Summary.java
OrderGenerator.java
OrderProcessor.java

blocks.text:
The catch block in `process` is the right way to handle `InterruptedException`: restore the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` and stop what you were doing. Swallowing it silently makes threads impossible to cancel. Here we convert it into an unchecked exception because the caller (a task in some pool) cannot do anything else with a checked one.

#### The runner interface and the baseline

blocks.title: Runner.java
SequentialRunner.java

blocks.text: #### Variant 1: producer-consumer with a BlockingQueue

blocks.title: QueueRunner.java

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- The queue is **bounded** (`ArrayBlockingQueue`). When consumers are slower than the producer, `put` blocks the producer. That is back-pressure: memory use stays bounded instead of growing without limit, which is how an unbounded queue turns a slow downstream into an OutOfMemoryError.
- Shutdown uses a **poison pill**: a special sentinel object, one per consumer. Each consumer exits when it takes one. Comparing with `==` is intentional; it is the identity of that exact object that matters.
- Results go into a `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`, a thread-safe collection, so consumers do not need explicit locks.
- `join()` on every thread establishes a happens-before edge: after the joins, the main thread is guaranteed to see everything the workers wrote (see the memory model chapter).
- Threads have names (`consumer-0`). Always name threads you create; stack dumps become readable.

#### Variant 2: a thread pool

blocks.title: PoolRunner.java

blocks.text:
`invokeAll` submits every task and blocks until all are done, returning futures in the same order as the tasks. `f.get()` returns the value or throws `ExecutionException` wrapping whatever the task threw. The `finally` block always shuts the pool down, using the standard three steps in `shutdownGracefully`: `shutdown()` stops intake, `awaitTermination` waits, `shutdownNow()` interrupts the stragglers. Forgetting to shut down a fixed pool leaves non-daemon worker threads alive, and the JVM never exits.

#### Variant 3: CompletableFuture

blocks.title: FutureRunner.java

blocks.text:
Each order becomes a small pipeline: validate, then process, with `exceptionally` turning any failure into a rejected result. Both stages run on our own pool; passing the executor explicitly avoids silently using the shared `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, which is sized for CPU work, not blocking calls. `allOf(...).join()` waits for every future. A realistic extension would add a stage per external call (inventory, payment, notification).

#### Variant 4: virtual threads

blocks.title: VirtualRunner.java

blocks.text:
Virtual threads (Java 21, see the virtual threads chapter) are so cheap that you create one **per task** and never pool them. When a virtual thread blocks in `sleep` or on a socket, the JVM unmounts it from its carrier thread and runs another one. The try-with-resources block works because `ExecutorService` implements `AutoCloseable` since Java 19; `close()` waits for submitted tasks to finish.

#### The driver

blocks.title: Main.java

blocks.text: ### Running it

blocks.code:
$ rm -rf out testout
$ javac -d out $(find src -name '*.java')
$ java -cp out com.example.orders.app.Main
200 orders, 10 ms simulated latency each
sequential                2122 ms  ok=172 rejected=28 sum=22627 (matches baseline)
queue(8 consumers)         271 ms  ok=172 rejected=28 sum=22627 (matches baseline)
pool(8 threads)            264 ms  ok=172 rejected=28 sum=22627 (matches baseline)
completable(8 threads)     263 ms  ok=172 rejected=28 sum=22627 (matches baseline)
virtual threads             38 ms  ok=172 rejected=28 sum=22627 (matches baseline)
blocks.title: Compile and run all five variants

blocks.text: The timings above are typical for the build machine (2 CPU cores) and will differ on yours, but the pattern should be the same.

rows: each order waits for the previous one: 200 x 10 ms is just over 2 s
eight orders wait at once; about 8 times faster, the wait dominates
all 200 wait at once; no limit of 8 to hit
blocks.caption: Reading the result (timings are typical, not guaranteed).

blocks.text: The last column of every line says "matches baseline": the accepted and rejected counts and the checksum are identical. Without that check, a faster-but-wrong implementation would look like a win.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Do not write micro-benchmarks like this and then quote them as facts about Java. A single cold run includes JIT warm-up, thread start cost and noise. We use it to see an order-of-magnitude effect (about 8x and then about 80x), which is large enough to survive the noise. For real measurements use JMH, the benchmark harness from the OpenJDK project.

### Graceful shutdown

Real services must stop cleanly: finish what is running, refuse new work, and report what was dropped. `ShutdownDemo` queues 40 tasks of 50 ms on 4 threads, waits a short time, then stops the pool.

blocks.title: ShutdownDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java -cp out com.example.orders.app.ShutdownDemo
clean shutdown : false
completed      : 12
interrupted    : 4
never started  : 24
accounted for  : 40
blocks.title: Run the shutdown demo (typical output)

blocks.text:
The exact split between completed, interrupted and never-started varies from run to run because it depends on timing, but the **accounted for** line must always equal 40: no task disappears silently. `shutdownNow()` returns the queued tasks that never began, so you can log or persist them. Tasks already running get an interrupt; they stop quickly only because `OrderProcessor` reacts to interruption. A task that ignores interrupts (a tight CPU loop that never checks the flag) will keep running regardless.

In a real application you would hook this into JVM shutdown with `Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(...)`, so that Ctrl+C or a container stop signal triggers the same three steps.

### Why shared counters are dangerous

The processors above never share mutable counters. Here is what happens when you do. Four threads each increment four counters 250,000 times.

blocks.title: RaceDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java -cp out com.example.orders.app.RaceDemo
plain int       : 967756
volatile int    : 968756
AtomicInteger   : 1000000
LongAdder       : 1000000
blocks.title: Run the race demo (typical output; plain and volatile vary)

blocks.text:
`plain++` is read, add one, write: three steps. Two threads can read the same value and both write back the same result, so updates are **lost**. `volatile` guarantees visibility of the latest write, but does not make the three steps atomic, so it loses updates too. `AtomicInteger` uses a compare-and-set instruction and is exact. `LongAdder` keeps several cells to reduce contention and sums them on demand; it is the best choice for a hot statistics counter that is written often and read rarely. If your run happened to print exactly 1,000,000 for the first two, that is luck, not correctness; the bug is still there.

### Tests

Concurrent code is tested by checking **properties that must hold on every schedule**, not exact interleavings: all runners agree with the baseline, no id is lost or duplicated, and the system terminates. Tests use a 1 ms latency to stay fast. The queue test with capacity 1 and 16 consumers is a stress shape: a tiny queue and many consumers force constant blocking and wake-ups, which is where shutdown bugs show up.

blocks.title: OrderTests.java

blocks.code:
$ javac -d testout -cp out $(find test -name '*.java')
$ java -cp out:testout com.example.orders.OrderTests
PASS business rules: limit and blocked customer
PASS generator is deterministic
PASS queue(4 consumers) matches the sequential baseline
PASS pool(4 threads) matches the sequential baseline
PASS completable(4 threads) matches the sequential baseline
PASS virtual threads matches the sequential baseline
PASS queue runner copes with a tiny queue and many consumers
PASS interrupt makes the processor fail fast and keeps the flag
8 tests, 0 failed
blocks.title: Run the tests
Watch out
blocks.text: A passing concurrency test is weak evidence. Races depend on timing and may fail one run in a thousand. Run such tests many times (a loop in the shell is enough), keep thread counts above the CPU count to provoke interleavings, and prefer designs that are correct by construction (no shared mutable state, immutable messages, thread-safe collections) over designs you have to test into confidence.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: When would you pick a platform-thread pool, and when virtual threads? Virtual threads suit many concurrent tasks that mostly block on I/O (HTTP calls, database queries): create one per task and do not pool them. A bounded pool of platform threads suits CPU-bound work (size about the number of cores) or when you must cap concurrency against a limited resource such as a database. Virtual threads do not make computation faster, and a semaphore is the tool for limiting them, not a small pool.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring Boot 3.2+ can run request handling on virtual threads with one property (`spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`). The service code stays blocking and simple, which is the appeal: you get thread-per-request readability with close to reactive scalability for I/O-bound services.

### Extension ideas

1. Add a `StructuredTaskScope` variant (preview in Java 21 and later releases; run with `--enable-preview`) and compare error handling.
2. Add retries: an order whose charge "times out" (random failure) is retried up to three times with a delay; count retries in a `LongAdder`.
3. Limit in-flight payments to 20 with a `Semaphore` in the virtual-thread variant.
4. Add a priority: premium customers' orders jump the queue using `PriorityBlockingQueue`.
5. Make the consumer count a command-line argument and plot (by hand) time against 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 threads. Where does it stop improving, and why?
6. Replace `ConcurrentLinkedQueue` for results with a per-thread list merged at the end, and think about which is faster and why.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Separate the work from the scheduling; compare every concurrent version against a sequential baseline using an order-independent summary.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Bounded queues give back-pressure; poison pills (one per consumer) give a clean stop; always join or close to get happens-before.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Shut down in three steps: `shutdown`, `awaitTermination`, `shutdownNow`, and make tasks respond to interruption.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Blocking I/O workloads gain from many threads; virtual threads make "one thread per task" affordable. Shared counters need atomics.

sections.title: Project D: An in-memory key-value store

blocks.text:
### Goal

Redis, Memcached and the caches inside every web framework are, at heart, a map with rules: values can expire, memory is bounded, and many threads use it at once. This project builds a small version and exposes it through a text shell:

**Shell commands**

blocks.code:
SET token abc123 100     store a value that expires after 100 ms
GET token                read it, or (nil)
INCR visits              atomic counter
DEL / SIZE / KEYS / PURGE

blocks.text:
You will build **three** store implementations behind one interface, so you can compare designs side by side:

1. `LockedStore`: a `HashMap` protected by a `ReentrantReadWriteLock`.
2. `ConcurrentStore`: a `ConcurrentHashMap` with no explicit locks.
3. `LruStore`: a size-bounded cache using `LinkedHashMap` in access order.

A background `ExpiryCleaner` built on `ScheduledExecutorService` removes dead entries, and the same contract tests run against every implementation.

### Design

- **Interface first.** `KeyValueStore` lists the operations: `put` (with optional TTL, time to live), `get`, `delete`, `incr`, `size`, `keys`, `purgeExpired`. Every implementation must obey the same contract; the tests enforce it.
- **Entries are immutable records.** `Entry(value, expiresAtMillis)`. To change a value you replace the entry. Immutable entries are safe to share between threads without locking.
- **Time is injected** as a `LongSupplier` of milliseconds. Production passes `System::currentTimeMillis`; tests pass a clock they control and call `advance(100)` instead of sleeping. Tests that sleep are slow and flaky.
- **Two kinds of expiry.** *Lazy*: `get` treats an expired entry as missing. *Active*: the cleaner periodically calls `purgeExpired`. Lazy expiry alone would leave dead entries in memory forever if nobody reads them; active expiry alone would return stale data between sweeps. Real caches (Redis included) use both.
- **Strings only.** Values are strings without spaces so the shell parser stays tiny. A real store would use bytes and a proper protocol.

### The code

#### Entry and the interface

blocks.title: Entry.java
KeyValueStore.java

blocks.text:
An expiry time of `0` means "never". The check `nowMillis >= expiresAtMillis` means an entry is dead **at** its expiry instant, not after it; a test pins that boundary down.

#### Version 1: HashMap plus ReadWriteLock

blocks.title: LockedStore.java

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- A `ReadWriteLock` allows **many readers at once or one writer alone**. For read-heavy workloads this beats a single `synchronized` because readers do not block each other. `get`, `size` and `keys` take the read lock; everything that changes the map takes the write lock.
- Every `lock()` is paired with `unlock()` in a `finally` block. If an exception escapes between them, the lock must still be released, or the next caller blocks forever.
- `get` does **not** delete an expired entry. Removing needs the write lock, and a read lock cannot be upgraded to a write lock: trying to take the write lock while holding the read lock **deadlocks** the thread against itself. So the read path only hides dead entries, and `purgeExpired` (write lock) removes them.
- `incr` is read-modify-write. It must happen under one write lock; two separate calls "get, then put" would lose updates.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: `ReentrantReadWriteLock` is not always faster than a plain lock. Taking a read lock still updates shared state, so with very short critical sections (like a `HashMap.get`) the lock bookkeeping costs more than the work it protects. It pays off when the protected work is longer, or reads vastly outnumber writes.
#### Version 2: ConcurrentHashMap

blocks.title: ConcurrentStore.java

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- There are no locks in our code. `ConcurrentHashMap` makes each single-key operation (`get`, `put`, `remove`, `compute`) atomic internally, using compare-and-swap for empty buckets and short per-bucket locking otherwise (see the concurrent collections chapter).
- `get` can safely remove an expired entry using the **two-argument** `map.remove(key, e)`, which removes only if the key is still mapped to that exact entry. Between our `get` and our `remove`, another thread may have stored a fresh value; the conditional remove leaves it alone. This is the check-then-act race solved with one atomic call.
- `incr` uses `compute`, which runs our lambda atomically for that key. The lambda must be short and must not touch the same map. The one-element array `result` is the usual trick to get a value out of a lambda.
- `purgeExpired` iterates while other threads modify the map. That is allowed: `ConcurrentHashMap` iterators are *weakly consistent*, never throw `ConcurrentModificationException`, and may or may not see concurrent changes.
- `size()` here counts live entries, so it is O(n). The built-in `map.size()` would be cheap but would also count expired entries. Production stores keep counters; we keep the code simple.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: The classic bug is `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v);` on a concurrent map. Each call is atomic but the pair is not: two threads can both pass the check. Use `putIfAbsent`, `computeIfAbsent` or `compute`, which do the check and the write as one operation.

#### Version 3: a bounded LRU cache

An **LRU** (least recently used) cache holds at most N entries and, when full, evicts the one that has gone unused the longest. `LinkedHashMap` has this built in: constructed with `accessOrder = true`, it moves each accessed entry to the end of its internal linked list, and overriding `removeEldestEntry` lets you evict the head after each insert.

blocks.title: LruStore.java

blocks.text:
Here the lesson is the opposite of version 1: with access ordering, **even** `get` **modifies the map** (it relinks a node). A read lock would let several threads reorder the list at once and corrupt it. So every method is `synchronized`. If you need an LRU under heavy contention, real libraries (Caffeine) use sophisticated buffered designs; for most programs a synchronized `LinkedHashMap` is the right size of solution. The anonymous subclass of `LinkedHashMap` also demonstrates an inner class reading the outer instance's field (`LruStore.this.capacity`) and its own state, which you met in the nested classes chapter.

#### The background cleaner

blocks.title: ExpiryCleaner.java

blocks.text:
Points to study: the thread factory names the thread and marks it **daemon**, so a forgotten cleaner cannot keep the program alive. `scheduleWithFixedDelay` waits the period *after each run finishes*, so runs never overlap or pile up (`scheduleAtFixedRate` would try to catch up). The `try/catch` inside the task is essential: if a scheduled task throws, the executor silently cancels all future runs of it. The class implements `AutoCloseable` so try-with-resources shuts it down.

#### The command shell

blocks.title: Shell.java
Main.java

blocks.text:
The shell returns a string for each command instead of printing, so it can be tested. The `switch` expression with `yield` gives each branch a value. `Locale.ROOT` in `toUpperCase` avoids the Turkish-i problem described in the Unicode chapter (a command `get` must map to `GET` on every machine). Errors from bad input come back as `ERR ...` text, never as exceptions that kill the loop. `Main` picks the implementation from a command-line argument, which is the strategy pattern in its simplest form.

### Running it

Save the session below as `session.txt`. The `SLEEP` command makes the shell pause so a 100 ms entry really expires and the cleaner runs.

**session.txt**

blocks.code:
SET name asha
GET name
SET token abc123 100
GET token
INCR visits
INCR visits
GET visits
SIZE
SLEEP 250
GET token
SIZE
DEL name
DEL name
GET name
SET a
FLY away
KEYS
QUIT

$ rm -rf out testout
$ javac -d out $(find src -name '*.java')
$ java -cp out com.example.kv.shell.Main < session.txt
store: ConcurrentStore
> SET name asha
OK
> GET name
"asha"
> SET token abc123 100
OK
> GET token
"abc123"
> INCR visits
(integer) 1
> INCR visits
(integer) 2
> GET visits
"2"
> SIZE
(integer) 3
> SLEEP 250
OK
> GET token
(nil)
> SIZE
(integer) 2
> DEL name
(integer) 1
> DEL name
(integer) 0
> GET name
(nil)
> SET a
ERR usage: SET key value [ttlMillis]
> FLY away
ERR unknown command 'FLY'
> KEYS
visits
cleaner removed 1 expired entries
blocks.title: Compile and run the default (ConcurrentStore)

blocks.text:
The SIZE before the sleep is 3 (name, token, visits); after, 2, because `token` expired. The final line shows the cleaner removed one entry. Whether the cleaner or the lazy `GET` removes an expired entry first depends on timing, so on your machine that count can be 0 or 1; the replies to the commands do not change either way.

Now the LRU variant with capacity 3. We touch `a` so that `b` becomes the eldest, then insert a fourth key:

**lru.txt**

blocks.code:
SET a 1
SET b 2
SET c 3
GET a
SET d 4
KEYS
QUIT

$ java -cp out com.example.kv.shell.Main lru < lru.txt
store: LruStore
> SET a 1
OK
> SET b 2
OK
> SET c 3
OK
> GET a
"1"
> SET d 4
OK
> KEYS
a c d
cleaner removed 0 expired entries
blocks.title: LRU eviction in action

blocks.text:
`b` is gone, although it was inserted before `c`; `a` survived because reading it counted as use.

### Tests

The tests have three layers. First, **contract tests** run in a loop over a list of factories, so each behaviour is asserted for all three stores with no copy-paste. Second, tests of behaviour unique to one class (LRU order, the cleaner thread). Third, the shell's parsing and error replies. A `ManualTime` clock makes expiry tests instant and exact.

blocks.title: KvTests.java

blocks.code:
$ javac -d testout -cp out $(find test -name '*.java')
$ java -cp out:testout com.example.kv.KvTests
PASS LockedStore: put, get, overwrite, delete
PASS LockedStore: entries expire after their ttl
PASS LockedStore: purgeExpired removes only expired entries
PASS LockedStore: incr is atomic across 4 threads
PASS ConcurrentStore: put, get, overwrite, delete
PASS ConcurrentStore: entries expire after their ttl
PASS ConcurrentStore: purgeExpired removes only expired entries
PASS ConcurrentStore: incr is atomic across 4 threads
PASS LruStore: put, get, overwrite, delete
PASS LruStore: entries expire after their ttl
PASS LruStore: purgeExpired removes only expired entries
PASS LruStore: incr is atomic across 4 threads
PASS LRU evicts the least recently used entry
PASS cleaner thread removes expired entries on its own
PASS shell parses commands and reports errors
PASS incr on a non-number value fails clearly
16 tests, 0 failed
blocks.title: Compile and run the tests

blocks.text:
The `incr` test starts four threads that each increment 10,000 times and expects exactly 40,000. If you replace the lock in `LockedStore.incr` by nothing, this test fails with a lower number; try it.

### Which one is faster? A measurement, and its limits

`Bench` runs 4 threads doing 4 million operations in total (95% reads) against the two concurrent stores, three rounds each.

blocks.code:
$ java -cp out com.example.kv.shell.Bench
round 1
  LockedStore        762 ms  (4000000 ops)
  ConcurrentStore    383 ms  (4000000 ops)
round 2
  LockedStore        489 ms  (4000000 ops)
  ConcurrentStore    379 ms  (4000000 ops)
round 3
  LockedStore        443 ms  (4000000 ops)
  ConcurrentStore    345 ms  (4000000 ops)
blocks.title: Throughput comparison (typical, noisy)

blocks.text: Read the numbers honestly. On the 2-core build machine neither store wins consistently; the differences between rounds are as large as the differences between stores. Much of the time is spent building the `"key" + n` strings and generating random numbers, not in the store. With 2 cores there is little real parallelism to exploit, and the first round includes JIT warm-up. The lesson is methodological: a hand-made benchmark can show *whether something is badly* *wrong*, not which of two similar designs is better. Use JMH (the OpenJDK Microbenchmark Harness) for real decisions, and decide on correctness and simplicity first: `ConcurrentStore` has less code, no locks to forget to release, and scales when cores are many.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Implement an LRU cache. What data structures and what complexity? A hash map for O(1) lookup plus a doubly linked list ordering keys by recency, with the map pointing into the list; get moves the node to the front, put inserts at the front and evicts the tail when over capacity: O(1) for both. In Java, `LinkedHashMap(capacity, 0.75f, true)` with `removeEldestEntry` does exactly this. Thread safety must be added separately, and note that `get` mutates the structure, so a read lock is not enough.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: `HashMap`, `Hashtable`, `Collections.synchronizedMap`, `ConcurrentHashMap`: the differences? `HashMap` is not thread-safe. `Hashtable` and `synchronizedMap` lock the whole map on every call and still need external locking for compound actions like iteration or check-then-put. `ConcurrentHashMap` locks at a much finer grain (CAS for empty bins, per-bin locks), allows lock-free reads, forbids null keys and values, and offers atomic compound operations (`compute`, `merge`, `putIfAbsent`).

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In production you would use Redis or Caffeine instead of writing your own. Spring Boot's cache abstraction (`@Cacheable`) plugs those in. Knowing how TTL, eviction and atomic counters work inside tells you what to configure and what failure modes to expect: a cache without a size bound or a TTL is a memory leak with a nice name.

### Extension ideas

1. Add an `EXPIRE key ms` command and a `TTL key` command that reports remaining milliseconds.
2. Persist the store: write a snapshot to a file on `SAVE` and load it at startup; skip entries that already expired. Reuse the write-then-rename trick from the bank project.
3. Make `LruStore` evict expired entries before live ones, using `purgeExpired` when the map is full.
4. Replace `size()`'s O(n) scan with an `AtomicInteger` or `LongAdder` maintained on put and delete. What race makes it hard with TTL?
5. Serve the shell over TCP: a `ServerSocket` that creates a virtual thread per connection and uses one shared store (see the networking mentions in Part 5).
6. Add a `MULTI`/`EXEC`-like batch that applies several commands atomically in `LockedStore` by holding the write lock, and explain why `ConcurrentStore` cannot do that cheaply.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Design to an interface and run one contract test suite against every implementation.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: `ReadWriteLock` helps read-heavy code but cannot upgrade a read lock; `ConcurrentHashMap` needs atomic compound operations (`compute`, `putIfAbsent`, conditional `remove`) instead of check-then-act.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: `LinkedHashMap` with access order and `removeEldestEntry` is a three-line LRU, but because `get` mutates it, guard it with a single lock.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Combine lazy and active expiry; run the cleaner on a daemon scheduled thread and catch exceptions inside it.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text: Inject time so tests are fast and exact; hand-made benchmarks show gross problems only.
#### How to work through the projects

items.question: Why does the project pass a `Clock` into the service instead of calling `LocalDate.now()` inside it?
items.answer: A fixed clock makes dates deterministic, so tests and book output never change from day to day.

items.question: Source file `src/com/example/bank/model/Account.java` declares `package com.example.bank.models;`. What goes wrong and where?
items.answer: javac compiles it, but the class file lands in `out/com/example/bank/models/` and other classes importing `...model.Account` will not find it; the error appears when compiling or running the importing code. Directory and package should match.

items.question: What does `javac -d out` do that plain `javac` does not?
items.answer: It writes class files into the given directory, creating directories that match the packages; without it they land next to the sources.

items.question: Why does a test runner need to call `System.exit` with a non-zero code on failure?
items.answer: Build servers and shell scripts decide success from the exit code; printing FAIL alone would still look like success to `&&` chains and CI.

blocks.text: #### Project A: A bank account manager

items.question: In `Account`, what happens if `history()` returned the field directly, and how would you notice in the tests?
items.answer: Callers could mutate or clear the history; the "history view cannot be modified" test would fail because no `UnsupportedOperationException` is thrown.

items.question: What does this print? `System.out.println(Money.format(-5) + " " + Money.format(1005));`
items.answer: `-0.05 10.05` (verified by the unit test for the first value; the second follows the same formula).

items.question: Why does `transfer` call `get(to)` before `src.withdraw(...)`?
items.answer: So an unknown destination fails before any money moves; otherwise the source would already be debited.

items.question: Why is `InsufficientFundsException` checked while `InvalidAmountException` is not?
items.answer: Running out of money is an expected business outcome callers must handle; a negative amount is a caller bug or bad input.

items.question: What is the purpose of writing a `.tmp` file and then moving it?
items.answer: A crash while writing leaves only a half-written `.tmp`; the rename is atomic, so the real file is always complete.

items.question: What is wrong with this alternative, and why? `catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("ERROR"); }` around the whole dispatch.
items.answer: It hides the cause (message lost), swallows programming bugs such as `NullPointerException`, and treats business declines like errors. Catch the specific exceptions you can handle.

blocks.text: #### Project B: A log file analyzer

items.question: What does this print? `Optional.of(1).stream().count() + Optional.empty().stream().count()`
items.answer: `1` (a present Optional streams one element, an empty one streams none; 1 + 0 as longs).

items.question: Why is `Pattern` a `static final` field in `LogParser` and not created inside `parse`?
items.answer: Compiling a regex is expensive and `Pattern` is immutable and thread-safe, so one shared instance is correct and faster; only `Matcher` is per-use and not thread-safe.

items.question: What is the difference between `Matcher.matches()` and `Matcher.find()`?
items.answer: `matches()` requires the entire input to match; `find()` looks for the next match anywhere inside.

items.question: What is wrong with `Stream<String> s = Files.lines(p); return s.count();` in a long-running program?
items.answer: The stream (and its file handle) is never closed; use try-with-resources.

items.question: In the analyzer, why is `partitioningBy` a better fit than `groupingBy` for the success-versus-failure split?
items.answer: It is for a boolean split and always returns both keys, so there are no missing-key surprises and the intent (two buckets) is clear.

items.question: Two entries have the same latency. Why does the "slowest" sort add `.thenComparing(LogEntry::time)`?
items.answer: `sorted` on ties follows input order in the sequential case, but an explicit tie-breaker makes the result deterministic regardless of how the data was produced.

blocks.text: #### Project C: A concurrent order processor

items.question: What does `ExecutorService.shutdown()` do to tasks already queued? And `shutdownNow()`?
items.answer: `shutdown()` lets queued and running tasks finish but accepts no new ones. `shutdownNow()` drops the queue (returning those tasks), and interrupts running tasks.

items.question: Why does the producer put one poison pill per consumer instead of just one?
items.answer: A consumer exits after taking one pill and never takes another. With N consumers, one pill would stop only one of them and the rest would block on `take` forever.

items.question: What is wrong with this handler, and what should it do? `catch (InterruptedException e) { }`
items.answer: It swallows the interrupt, so the thread cannot be cancelled. Restore the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` or propagate the exception, and stop the work.

items.question: Four threads each run `count++` on a shared `volatile int` 1000 times. Can the final value be less than 4000? Why?
items.answer: Yes. `count++` is read-modify-write; `volatile` ensures visibility but not atomicity, so concurrent increments can be lost (use `AtomicInteger` or `LongAdder`).

items.question: Why pass an explicit executor to `supplyAsync` for blocking work?
items.answer: The default common pool has about as many threads as cores; blocking tasks would occupy them and starve other CompletableFuture work in the JVM.

items.question: Why is the queue in `QueueRunner` bounded?
items.answer: To apply back-pressure: a fast producer blocks instead of filling memory with queued orders.

blocks.text: #### Project D: An in-memory key-value store

items.question: Why can `LockedStore.get` not simply call `map.remove(key)` when it finds an expired entry?
items.answer: It holds only the read lock, and a read lock cannot be upgraded to a write lock; requesting it deadlocks. Also, removing under a read lock would be a data race with other readers.

items.question: What is the bug? `if (!map.containsKey(k)) { map.put(k, 1); }` where `map` is a `ConcurrentHashMap`.
items.answer: Check-then-act race: two threads can both see the key absent and both put. Use `putIfAbsent` or `compute`.

items.question: Why would a `ReadWriteLock` be wrong for the LRU cache?
items.answer: In access order `get` relinks nodes, i.e. it writes to the map, so concurrent "readers" would corrupt the list. Use `synchronized` or a write lock.

items.question: What does this print? `var m = new LinkedHashMap<String,Integer>(16, 0.75f, true); m.put("a",1);` `m.put("b",2); m.get("a"); System.out.println(m.keySet());`
items.answer: `[b, a]`, because the `get("a")` moved `a` to the most-recent end (verify in jshell).

items.question: What happens to a `scheduleWithFixedDelay` task whose body throws an uncaught exception?
items.answer: The executor suppresses the exception and never runs the task again, silently. Catch exceptions inside the task.

items.question: Why do the tests use a manual clock instead of `Thread.sleep`?
items.answer: A manual clock makes expiry exact, instant and deterministic; sleeping makes tests slow and flaky on busy machines.
